opus-5.5.text:
I think each of them played a quite different role, and together they shaped the open-source ecosystem we have today.

Llama was really the starting point. When Meta released the first Llama in early 2023, it was the first time many researchers, in academia and in smaller companies, had access to a reasonably strong base model they could actually touch: fine-tune it, study it, build on it. Before that, if you weren't inside a big lab, you mostly read papers and imagined what these models were like. Llama turned large models from something you watched from outside into something you could work on. A huge number of derivative projects, like instruction tuning, alignment experiments, and quantization tools, grew out of that. So I'd say Llama's contribution was opening the door and starting the ecosystem.

Qwen's contribution, I think, is breadth and consistency. They kept releasing models across many sizes, from very small to very large, plus multimodal, code, and math variants, and kept iterating at a steady pace. That matters a lot for real adoption. Developers need a model that fits their hardware, their language, and their use case, and they need to trust that it'll keep being updated. Qwen became the default base for many people, especially in the Chinese-speaking community and then globally. That's ecosystem building through reliability and coverage, and it's not easy.

DeepSeek's contribution, from my perspective, was showing that open source can push the frontier itself, not just follow. The emphasis was on technical innovation under constraints: architecture choices like MLA and fine-grained MoE, training efficiency, and later showing with reasoning models that you could reach strong capability with a very transparent recipe and publish the details openly. The point wasn't only releasing weights, but releasing understanding, like how it was done and why, so others could reproduce and build on it. That changed people's beliefs about what's possible with limited compute, and about whether open models could be close to the best closed ones.

So, in short: Llama opened the door, Qwen built the house that a lot of people live in, and DeepSeek showed that the open community could also be the one drawing new blueprints. These roles are complementary, and the field benefited from all three.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the three played quite different roles, and it helps to look at them in order, because each one shifted what "open source" meant in practice.

Llama was the starting gun. When Meta released the first Llama in early 2023, and then Llama 2 that summer with a license you could actually build products on, it did something no one else with that level of resources was willing to do. It said, here is a strong base model, take it. Before that, the open community was working with models that were clearly a tier below what the big labs had. Llama closed that gap enough that an entire ecosystem could form around it: fine-tuning recipes, quantization, inference frameworks like llama.cpp, the whole Alpaca and Vicuna lineage. Almost everything in open-source LLM tooling in 2023 was built on the assumption that the weights looked like Llama's. So Llama's contribution was less about any single technical idea and more about creating the substrate. It made open models a serious category.

Qwen, to me, is the contribution of consistency and coverage. What Alibaba did, starting with Qwen in late 2023 and then much more aggressively through Qwen1.5, Qwen2, and Qwen2.5, was to ship an entire family, from very small models you could run on a phone up to large ones, across base, chat, code, math, vision, and audio, all under a permissive license and all with a reasonably predictable release cadence. That matters a lot for practitioners. If you are a developer, you do not just want one great model, you want a size that fits your budget and a modality that fits your problem, and you want to trust that the next version will be there in a few months. Qwen also did a lot for multilingual capability, especially Chinese and other Asian languages, which Llama was weak on for a long time. In a sense Qwen became the default open model for a large part of the world the same way Llama was in the US.

DeepSeek is the one I obviously have the most personal perspective on, so I'll try to be fair rather than partial. I think DeepSeek's contribution was to open up the frontier research itself, not just the weights. From DeepSeek LLM in late 2023 through DeepSeek-V2, V3, and then R1, the releases came with technical reports that actually explained the ideas: multi-head latent attention, the particular way we did fine-grained mixture of experts with shared experts, the auxiliary-loss-free load balancing, the FP8 training details, and later the reinforcement learning recipe behind R1. A lot of labs publish weights but keep the interesting engineering vague. DeepSeek published the engineering. And the second thing was cost. Showing that you could train a model competitive with the closed frontier for a fraction of what people assumed it required changed the conversation about who gets to participate in this. That had an effect on the whole industry, including on how Llama and Qwen approached their later releases.

So if I compress it: Llama proved open weights could be good enough to matter. Qwen proved an open family could be broad, reliable, and global. DeepSeek proved that open research could sit at the frontier and that the frontier was cheaper than people thought. They reinforced each other. Each one raised expectations, and the others responded. I think that competitive dynamic, more than any single release, is the real story of open-source models since 2023.

astra-6.text:
I think they made different kinds of contributions. Llama’s biggest contribution was to open up a starting point. Beginning in 2023, it showed the community that you could take a strong pretrained model and build on it. That helped an entire ecosystem develop around fine-tuning, inference, and evaluation. Strictly speaking, open weights and open source aren’t identical, but the practical impact was enormous.

Qwen contributed through sustained development and breadth. It gave developers a strong multilingual model family, particularly for Chinese, with different sizes and capabilities that could serve real applications. That continuity matters: people need an ecosystem they can keep building with.

DeepSeek’s contribution, as I see it, has been to explore technical approaches that improve capability while making training and inference more efficient, and to share enough technical detail for others to learn from those approaches. Releasing weights lets people use a model; explaining the decisions behind it helps the community advance.

So I wouldn’t describe this as one team replacing another. Llama helped establish the foundation, Qwen broadened what developers could build, and DeepSeek pushed further on efficiency and technical openness. Those contributions reinforce one another.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they made different contributions at different stages. Llama helped establish the foundation: it showed what capable open-weight models could make possible and gave the community a common starting point for experimentation. People could work on fine-tuning, deployment, and applications without training everything from scratch.

Qwen contributed through sustained development and a broad model ecosystem, especially for Chinese and multilingual use. That continuity matters. Developers need models they can use, adapt, and keep building on.

DeepSeek’s contribution, as I see it, has been to explore technical approaches and share enough detail for others to learn from them. Releasing weights is valuable, but explaining the architectural and training choices makes that release more useful to researchers.

So I wouldn’t see this simply as a competition over who has the strongest model. These contributions reinforce one another: a shared foundation brings more people in, a broad ecosystem makes the models useful, and technical openness helps the whole community move forward.
